authoredPrompt: This figure is a ball-and-stick model of a single sulfuric acid molecule, H2SO4, floating on a plain white field with no labels beyond the atom symbols. A yellow sphere labeled "S" sits at the center, and four red spheres labeled "O" radiate from it in a tetrahedral arrangement rendered in perspective: one up and slightly left, one out to the left, one down and toward the viewer, and one to the right. Each sulfur-oxygen bond is a cylinder colored yellow on the sulfur half and red on the oxygen half. Two of the oxygens carry a small white sphere labeled "H" on a short red-and-white bond: the upper one, whose hydrogen points up and right, and the right-hand one, whose hydrogen points up and slightly left. The other two oxygens are terminal and bare. Equal bond lengths and roughly equal angles about the sulfur make the tetrahedral geometry the thing to read off the model, while hydrogen on exactly two oxygens separates the hydroxyl pair from the pair that is not protonated. The structure is that of the compound industry manufactures in greater quantity than any other.
authoredInteractions:
- Click an oxygen atom to classify it as hydroxyl or terminal; the selected O-H bond or bare S-O bond highlights, making clear that only two of the four oxygens carry hydrogens.
- Toggle between atom-label and bond-type overlays: the molecule switches from S/O/H labels to colored S-O and O-H bond emphasis, making clear how the same tetrahedral framework contains two acidic hydroxyl groups.
authoredContext:
The preparation of sulfuric acid, H2SO4 (shown in the figure), begins with the oxidation of sulfur to sulfur trioxide and then converting the trioxide to sulfuric acid. Pure sulfuric acid is a colorless, oily liquid that freezes at 10.5 °C. It fumes when heated because the acid decomposes to water and sulfur trioxide. The heating process causes the loss of more sulfur trioxide than water, until reaching a concentration of 98.33% acid. Acid of this concentration boils at 338 °C without further change in concentration (a constant boiling solution) and is commercially concentrated H2SO4. The amount of sulfuric acid used in industry exceeds that of any other manufactured compound.

Sulfuric acid has a tetrahedral molecular structure.

A space filling model shows a yellow atom labeled, “S,” bonded on four sides to red atoms labeled, “O.” Two of the red atoms are bonded to white atoms labeled, “H.”

The strong affinity of concentrated sulfuric acid for water makes it a good dehydrating agent. It is possible to dry gases and immiscible liquids that do not react with the acid by passing them through the acid.
